title: Chapter 55: Five Girls
html:
The chair stood in the center of the corridor. To explore the second floor, Chen Ge would have to pass it. He had not forgotten what happened at the girls’ dormitory; these chairs seemed drawn to the living.

He hesitated in the stairwell.

It has a proper backrest and looks different from the other chairs in this building. Someone must have moved it here from elsewhere, but why?

On closer inspection, it resembled the one in the girls’ dormitory, probably part of the furniture once assigned to its rooms.

Using his phone’s camera, Chen Ge zoomed in on a door sign. It appeared to designate a vocal-training room. The dance studio isn’t on this floor. Should I go straight to the third? But what if another chair is waiting up there? If they both start chasing me, I’ll be trapped between them.

The image decided him. He entered the second-floor corridor. Shadows swallowed its far end, every door was closed, and dust filmed the windows so thickly that he could not see through them.

He advanced at a measured pace. The chair’s possible threat did not tempt him to rush; the abandoned classrooms on either side frightened him more.

How long has it been since anyone living set foot here? The dust is so thick that I can’t hide my footprints. If whoever is following me enters this building, they’ll know exactly where I went.

Even here, he had not forgotten the unknown person outside. I need to finish this as quickly as possible.

His phone’s light wavered with every movement as he edged toward the chair.

There’s nothing frightening about it, right? What can a wooden chair do?

He circled it. Up close, it seemed to be nothing more than an ordinary wooden chair.

Maybe I should take a closer look at it…

Before the thought had fully formed, he tipped the chair onto its side. Handwriting marked its underside.

Qian Yujiao? That sounds like the name of a girl.

The name confirmed his suspicion. This was not furniture from the Arts Activities Center but a chair that had belonged to a particular student. When the school held large events, students must have brought chairs from their own rooms and written their names underneath to avoid confusion.

Does that mean the chair in the girls’ dormitory has a name underneath it too?

Chen Ge committed the name to memory. After some hesitation, he spared the chair and moved it into an empty classroom. The longer I stay, the worse this place feels. I should get to the third floor.

He retraced his steps and climbed to the third floor. This corridor was empty. In the classrooms he checked, desks and chairs had been piled against the rear walls. Patches of fresh paint stood out clearly from the older, discolored surface.

If the school was already closing, why waste money repainting the walls? Who was this for?

His experience at Ping An Apartments suggested one answer. They were hiding something.

He scraped away some paint with the mallet, but the wall beneath was perfectly ordinary—no bloodstains, no strange markings.

No, there has to be something more than this.

As he searched the other rooms, a pattern emerged. Only certain patches had been repainted, many of them suspiciously close to the indoor pipes.

The building’s drainage system was probably renovated shortly before it closed.Chen Ge studied the pipes. The rooms on the first and second floors were clearly in use, but the third floor seems to have been abandoned even before the school shut down.

Desks and chairs stood piled together, not a single piece of chalk remained on the lecterns, and several classrooms had been locked.

Ghost haunting? Murder? Hidden security concern?

Any number of things might have led the school to seal off the floor, and Chen Ge lacked the evidence to choose among them. He left the classroom and headed for the fourth floor.

After the first step, he glanced back to see whether the wooden chair had followed him.

It had not.

At the landing between the third and fourth floors, a rope stretched between the banisters. A wooden board hung from it, bearing the same warning as the sign outside: NO ENTRY.

The sign did not deter him. He moved it aside and ducked beneath the rope.

At the top of the stairs, a faded sign hung from the door directly opposite him.

The dance studio!

At last he had found the place most likely to contain the red dancing shoes. Unlike the floors below, the fourth had no separate classrooms; interior walls had been removed to create one large studio.

Chen Ge tore away the seals, forced the lock, and opened a door that had remained shut for years. Time seemed to have forgotten the room. Everything stood as it had on the day the school closed.

A film of dust covered the polished floor, and a peculiar odor filled the studio—like strong deodorant gone rancid after years in a sealed room.

Keeping close to the wall, he entered. The studio had been professionally equipped, with a waxed wooden floor for dance practice and acoustic panels to keep the noise from disturbing other classes.

This is the first time I’ve seen such a large dance studio.

He used his phone’s camera to examine the room. Adjustable ballet barres lined the walls, with a row of low benches beneath them.

Six full-length mirrors covered the opposite wall, joined edge to edge. Each was roughly a meter wide and two meters tall.

I’d almost forgotten that mirrors are a necessary fixture inside a dance studio.

The row of mirrors made him draw a slow breath. Then he noticed three wooden chairs positioned before their center.

Three at once?

Biting his lip, he approached. The mirrors repeated his every movement.

Alone in an empty dance studio at midnight, facing six versions of himself, Chen Ge felt his unease deepen.

He resisted the urge to smash the glass and tipped the chairs onto their sides. Like the one downstairs, each bore a girl’s name underneath.

Including the chair in the girls’ dormitory, I’ve found five. If each represents one girl, then I’m dealing with five spirits. What happened to them?
